summary:
Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament in Protestant Bibles. The name is Hebrew for "my messenger," the same word God uses in 3:1; whether it is a proper name or an anonymous title is debated — the book names no father, hometown, or date (1:1). The setting is after the exile: the temple is standing, sacrifices are running, and Judah has a Persian-appointed "governor" (1:8). Its abuses — defective offerings, careless priests, intermarriage, withheld tithes — are the ones Nehemiah fought in the mid-400s BC (Nehemiah 13), where many interpreters date the book.

The book is built as disputations, back-and-forth arguments usually counted as six: God states a charge, the people object, God answers. "I have loved you," says the LORD (1:2); the people reply, "How have You loved us?" It repeats: "How have we despised Your name?" (1:6); "How do we rob You?" (3:8). Priests accept blind, lame, and sick animals: "Try offering them to your governor!" (1:8). Men break faith with "the wife of your youth" (2:14) — "For I hate divorce," says the LORD (2:16). The tithe — the tenth owed to support the temple and its ministers — is withheld, and some conclude, "It is futile to serve God" (3:14).

The rebukes carry promises. On the tithe: "Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house. Test Me in this... See if I will not open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure" (3:10). To "Where is the God of justice?" (2:17) God answers: "Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple" (3:1) — quoted of John the Baptist in Mark 1:2. The Lord who comes will be "like a refiner's fire" (3:2) and will purify "the sons of Levi" until offerings again please the LORD (3:3–4).

The last chapter faces both directions: back — "Remember the law of My servant Moses" (4:4) — and forward — "I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD" (4:5) — the prophets' term for God's decisive intervention to judge and restore. The New Testament links this Elijah to John the Baptist ("he is the Elijah who was to come," Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13), and the angel announcing John's birth echoes Malachi's closing line about turning "the hearts of the fathers to their children" (4:6; Luke 1:17).
